Mr. Hayman, I believe that you must continue with your questions and then the witness can make a general comment about any drawing that you wish to make. This, it seems to me, would be a better way to organise the work of the Tribunal. What is the opinion of the Prosecutor? I would like to have the opinion if Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, your Honours, I think the witness is making his position quite clear in respect of the intertwined relationship between the military and civilian authorities, and I think he infers that it is extraordinarily difficult to actually represent that graphically at the top. My own view would be that learned counsel should move on with his questioning, that that is a matter for you. I think that is what the witness is now indicating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Pause.) Mr. Hayman, the Tribunal would like you to make your drawing. The witness wanted to co-operate with you but can't. He explained his position. We give you three minutes to make your drawing, which will be commented on by the witness, and then we will move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't make a drawing based on his testimony to date, because it's unclear to me. I'll ask a couple more questions in this area and move on, if it's acceptable to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree, Dr. Pajic, that a distinction is drawn within the decrees in Exhibit 38 between the Department of Defence and the army of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a distinction. The Department is just a part of the government cabinet, as we can call the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the Department of Defence answered to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree that the army answered to the Department of Defence in a hierarchical manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can draw those two elements on the chart. You would consent to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any comments or corrections to what I have drawn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Pajic. Thank you for putting up with my attempt to add clarity to your testimony. You did say in your testimony, by the way, that you found the decrees in Exhibit 38 to be clear, consistent and apparently written by someone with considerable legal skill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever undertaken a scholarly study of military institutions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever studied the issue of command and control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Have you ever studied the issue in a military context of the concept of command and control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you using the word "control" in the sense of the control of the military organisation by civilian bodies?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I mean within a military organisation the control of soldiers by commanders and the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have. It is an area I studied when studying international war law, but I did that, of course, at the academic level, without insight into any legal documents, but I was mainly reading literature on the subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the documents you were asked to look at in connection with this case, did you undertake a study of the issue of command and control within the army of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever studied the issue of institution building, that is creating an institution such as a military out of nothing, from scratch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not exclusively the building of military institutions, but I did study to some extent the process of development of state institutions as such in connection with the implementation of the Dayton accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not military institutions, I take it? You have never studied that aspect of their birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with this project or any other have you ever studied the decrees or decisions of any other organisation giving birth to a military, that is any other nascent military organisation, or are these the only decrees you have studied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are the only decrees that I have had occasion to study in this form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you have suggested that the formation of the HZ H-B reflected territorial ambitions; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have also suggested that those territorial ambitions were linked to ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it further your opinion that that development increased ethnic polarisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina during this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be one of the acceptable interpretations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it an interpretation that you would subscribe to as a political analyst and commentator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you please repeat your question regarding polarisation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that the formation of the HZ H-B increased ethnic polarisation within Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and to a high degree. I say that because at the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina an alliance was formed or a coalition between two leading political parties, on the one hand the party of the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the SDA, and on the other, the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HDZ. With the strengthening of the HZ H-B, the coalition was dealt a rather heavy blow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with the proposition that the Vance-Owen plan increased ethnic polarisation within Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm glad that you have asked me this question. The Vance-Owen plan was a comprehensive project for regulating Bosnia-Herzegovina. That would be based on a certain number of cantons. I think there were ten. These cantons were intended to ensure to a greater or lesser degree the majority authority of the people who were in the majority in certain areas or cantons, but I should like to recall that the Vance-Owen plan was a highly comprehensive document, which contained exceptional, exceptionally clear provisions regarding guarantees of human rights, basic freedoms, and especially the position of minorities in those cantons. Unfortunately, and I have written about this, I have written in some of my papers, the majority of participants in the negotiations in Geneva within the framework of the UN conference on the former Yugoslavia understood the Vance-Owen plan exclusively as maps, as maps delineating certain cantons, and that led many to believe that this was a sign for them to gain control of those territories, without paying any attention to the other provisions referring to the organisation of some sort of democratic authority giving guarantees for human rights. I had to make a rather lengthy answer to this question. I beg your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. You agree then, I take it, that the plan, at least as interpreted by the party to the ensuing conflict, increased ethnic polarisation an tensions; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In view of the way in which it was interpreted, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, you have written, have you not, that the cantons created by the Vance-Owen plan: " ... will likely lead to further large scale displacements as minority populations will flee"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is reminiscent of my position, but I would like to know which Article you are quoting from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the document be provided to the witness, your Honour, and I have copies for the court and counsel. (Handed)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, before we move to this document, do you want the drawing to be put in as an exhibit into the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does the Prosecutor agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Registrar, will you put it in after documents D1 and 2. This can become a new exhibit as soon as the other side as looked at it as well. This can then be entered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, if you would look at the document in front of you, and before we place the pertinent part on the ELMO, can you identify this as an article that you co-authored in January of 1993 and that was published in the Manchester Guardian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now perhaps, your Honour, the highlighted paragraph could be placed on the ELMO so that it may be translated. I am referring to the paragraph that begins with the words: "Most fundamentally ..." Perhaps the translators could let us know when the translation is concluded. (Pause.)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman, you can go on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Dr. Pajic, do you acknowledge the passage we have referred to as your own words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also agree with the proposition that the political activities of President Alija Izetbegovic increased ethnic polarisation within Bosnia and Herzegovina during this time period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What specific political moves are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I must ask your indulgence, and perhaps you can explain some of your earlier words. Could another article be provided to the witness, your Honour? (Handed) For the record, this is an article that appeared in the Manchester Guardian on August 2nd, 1993. Headline: "Wrong man in the wrong place". The portion that I wish to call the witness' attention to is highlighted in yellow, and appears at the bottom of the page marked page 20, carrying over to the top of the page marked page 21. First, Dr. Pajic, do you concede that you were interviewed and gave a statement in connection with this article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This article was written by Ian Trainor, Guardian reporter and correspondent for many years from Bosnia-Herzegovina. I had several meetings with him and probably during one of those conversations -- it may even have been by telephone -- he reproduced this sentence which figures in his article, but there is not much point in me complicating things now. In essence I accept that that is what I said at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the highlighted sentence be translated, starting on page 20? That will require the usher to turn the page at the appropriate time to page 21. (Pause.)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic, you provided us graciously with your curriculum vitae, which I believe learned counsel from the Prosecutor's Office said you prepared and provided to them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, by the way, is exhibit 35, the curriculum vitae of the witness. In your curriculum vitae as well as your testimony you have described, among other things, numerous consultancy relationships with United Nations' bodies and other third party bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever worked for the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Dr. Pajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never had any paid office or duty in the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I was a member of the Commission for Constitutional Matters of the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as I said, in 1991, and a part of 1992, and during the months of war in Sarajevo I attended several meetings, which were not really meetings of government bodies, but they were meetings of political institutions in Sarajevo. I must say again, though I'm speaking from memory, I must say that before the war, that is towards the end of the 1980s and during the election campaign in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990, and throughout the period up to my departure from Sarajevo, I enjoyed the reputation of an independent intellectual. I had very good working relationships with all the political parties, even with all three national parties, the SDA, the SDS and the HDZ, which I criticised in public, because of their nationalistic concepts. I had an open access to the media in Sarajevo. I was frequently interviewed by Sarajevo television, and though I was living in quite insufferable fear that my house, like many others, would be hit by a shell, I was invited from President Izetbegovic's cabinet by one of the diplomats of the former Yugoslavia, who started working at the time for the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Harudin Samun, who told me that Mr. Izetbegovic was asking me to join the State delegation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an expert for international law when this delegation went to the European Summit in Helsinki. This was a European Summit for the conference on security and co-operation in Europe which, as far as I can remember, took place in the first week of the month of July: I must explain this. I had a discussion at home with my wife and my closest friends over this invitation, and I was in a dilemma as to whether I should accept that invitation, because throughout the previous period I was quite a prominent opponent of national parties, including the Party of Democratic Action, of which Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was the President. However, after giving the matter some thought, I decided that, after all, in view of the significance of the meeting and in view of the situation in Sarajevo in the first place I felt it to be my morale duty as an expert for international law to take part in that delegation. I had a telephone conversation with Mr. Izetbegovic and I said that I accepted to participate in the delegation on condition that Sarajevo television should state that I was travelling to Helsinki as an independent expert for international law and not as an official of any state body. That's the whole story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it you served as a legal adviser to that delegation from Bosnia-Herzegovina, went to Helsinki with them and provided legal advice and guidance to them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was an ad hoc consultancy trip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that fact is reflected in the article from the London Times that has been placed to your right on the ELMO? Do you see this is dated July 14th, 1992. Paragraph 5 states: "Mr. Pajic, who was the legal adviser to the Bosnian government delegation at the CSCE talks in Helsinki last week". Do you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I went through your curriculum vitae and I couldn't find this consultancy and relationship with the government anywhere. Can you help me find it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not in my curriculum vitae and I know why. I did not enter in my CV any ad hoc engagements for any organisation, because, after all, for this type of consultancy there was no contact. There was no special appointment. It was simply a telephone call. I accepted the invitation. I went to Helsinki with the delegation for three days. I came back home and never since have I seen Mr. Izetbegovic even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that the documents and exhibits marked during the cross-examination of Dr. Pajic be admitted into evidence. I would like to thank Dr. Pajic for coming to the Tribunal and providing it with his views, important views, and with that the Defence has no further questions for Dr. Pajic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayman. Re-examination by Mr. Cayley

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before we give the floor to the Prosecutor for a brief reply, I would first like to ask the Registrar if he can tell us the numbering of the various documents that will fall under D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. There's D1, which is the first one that was given to the witness. Then there's D2, which is on the easel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: D2 is on the easel, but you could give some details about them. I'm sorry. D2 is the drawing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Then there is D3, D4 and D5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: These are the articles. They have to be indicated more specifically. We will not do them right now. We will think about stating exactly what they are. That is D2, 3 and 4. I think you wanted to use your right to ask several other questions of the witness. I ask you that this be done relatively quickly. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You have my understanding that I will be brief, Mr. President. Dr. Pajic, a few questions in general conclusion. From your research of all of the documents that the Office of the Prosecutor has put before you, is there any doubt in your mind that the entity of Herceg-Bosna from its commencement in November of 1991 aspired to statehood, which it ultimately attained when it declared itself a republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think you are right, and if you take that legislation as a continuous process, that particular aspiration could be clearly identified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whatever the catalyst for the creation of this entity, and Mr. Nobilo questioned you at some length and it's in the transcript, and he spoke of Serbs and used this pejorative term Cetnik, what were the prime aims of this entity from the start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The prime aim of the entity as it was defined in the decision of the establishment of HZ H-B was to circle a certain territory based on cultural, political, economic and territorial identity, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please try to ask questions that you have not already asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. In any of the documents that you have read, Dr. Pajic, is there any express reference which allows the participation of persons of non-Croat ethnicity in the governing organs of this entity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my recollection there is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind whatsoever that the HVO was in control of the executive, the judiciary, was a participant in the legislature and in charge of the armed forces of HZ H-B Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the founding principle of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The founding principle of the HVO is to be established as a supreme body of defence of HZ H-B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were to quantify the amount of documentation devoted to the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna, what would be your reply in everything that was provided to you by the office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A great amount of documents was dedicated to the armed forces, but I do not tend to look at it as a quantity but more as a quality, if you want, because the longest documents and the most substantial documents, in fact, are documents relating to the armed forces in general, like the document on the establishment of armed forces, the document on the military discipline, documents on ranks in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could very briefly refer you to document 2 in the index of documents, page 14, and if I could refer you to Article 11, could you read to the court the first sentence of that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to identify with no doubt it is a decree on armed forces, I take it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is correct, Dr. Pajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 11: "In order to perform the tasks stipulated in paragraph 2, Article 10 of this decree within the Defence Department a general staff shall be established".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is absolutely clear that the word "within" is used; is that correct? "Within the Defence Department a general staff shall be established"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The "General Staff" would be the translation of "Glavni Stoija".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO give itself powers to appropriate expropriate private and public property, including the property of private citizens, public enterprises on the territory which it claims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any of the documents that have been placed before you, is there any express contractual incorporation of international legislation guaranteeing the rights of minorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I referred yesterday in your testimony to the constitutional -- the day before yesterday, my apologies -- to the constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to the decision of the Supreme Court with regard to the Herceg-Bosna entity, and indeed Mr. Nobilo discussed with you at some length that particular decision. This is my last question. What was the position of the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina in respect of this entity that was created in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With due respect, Mr. Cayley, you are probably thinking of the Constitutional Court, not the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. The Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The position of the Constitutional Court expressed in the decision adopted, if I am not wrong, in September 1992, was that all the documents, decisions and decrees passed by HZ H-B in the period between November 1991 until December 1992 were unconstitutional, and they were declared to be illegal from the point of view of the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Nobilo agreed with you on that point. It's in the transcript. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, would you like to reply, but that will be the end? We agree that Mr. Hayman can have the final word here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Despite the fact there are a few minutes left, your Honour, I have no further questions. I would like to note, though, in response to Mr. Cayley's initial comment that Mr. Nobilo used an ethnically pejorative term in his cross-examination, the term will Nobilo used was read from the preamble of one of these decrees. He did not use it himself. He was quoting a document. I simply wish the record to be clear in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: My apologies. I meant no offence at all by that. I realise you were reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All of this will be included in the transcript. Thank you, Mr. Cayley, thank you Mr. Hayman. Mr. Pajic, you are not yet finished, because there are still some people who may want to ask you questions. Judge Riad would like to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Professor Pajic, I would just like to have some clarification concerning the minorities within the Croatian Community in Herceg-Bosna. You mentioned that there were strong communities of minorities, which varied between 7 per cent and 82 per cent according to the municipalities. What was this minority composed of in its majority? Could you answer me in your good English, so that I will not have to put this on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I stated that in 26 out of 30 municipalities listed in the decision of the establishment of HZ H-B 26 of those did not have an overall majority of Croat population. I'm not -- if you want me to, I can go through the data here, but those data are extracted from the census population of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for details, but basically they were formed of what communities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, generally, generally Bosnia-Herzegovina was -- consisted, and if I can say it still consisted of three constituent peoples, and that fact was confirmed by the Dayton accord, and those peoples are Croats, Muslims and Serbs, with a small change in terminology where Muslims are now called Bosniaks, but that's a completely different matter. A certain percentage of other nationalities also lived in those communities) and my assumption is that those others were people who would categorise themselves either as Yugoslavs, which meant in the Yugoslav terminology mostly people of mixed ethnic background, or in some of those municipalities you could have in addition to Croats, Muslims, Serbs and others, you could have probably Jews, probably some Montenegrins, people who had that kind of ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now they had no access to public office, as I understood. They could not participate in any representations, but they were subjected to the military duties; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the way I understood the documents here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Could you, according to your knowledge, clarify if this commitment, this participation in military duties was implemented in practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no information about that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Professor Pajic, if I may follow on from the last series of questions, we have this position outlined by you, if I understood your evidence correctly, that the constituent documents of the HZ H-B did not allow non-Croats to occupy governmental positions. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are, and I can quote two provisions, one referring to the composition of the Presidency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I really do not need you to quote them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I merely wanted to confirm with you the accuracy of my recollection of what you said. Now, that being correct, my question is this: was there anything in the constituent instrument of the HZ H-B which precluded or prohibited non-Croats from occupying governmental positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was nothing that would allow non-Croats to participate in the State institutions of HZ H-B; in other words, attached to the Presidency and later on to the House of Representatives of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna there were provisions providing or establishing that only representatives of Croat people could be the members of the Presidency or House of Representatives respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Am I right then in understanding the effect of your testimony to be this, that those provisions effectively excluded non-Croats from occupying governmental positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Okay. Now the second question, and there are only two questions I want to ask, has to do with an instrument to which you alluded some time ago. It is in the binder at tab 3, I think, and the endorsed numbering reads in the English text 00507600 at page 53. It probably is page 54 in the French text. I'm not sure. It is a decision on establishing the criteria for defining confidential defence data, etc. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I have in mind more particularly Article 13, which relates to official secrets. What I wanted to ask you, Professor, was whether this instrument is still in force so far as the HZ H-B is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no information that it has been repealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Then on presumption of continuity, it is still in force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Now the effect of this provision, as you explained it, would be this, to bar the disclosure of HZ H-B official secrets to the governmental authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Would that continue to be the position as at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may broaden my answer with just a few words. You will remember, your Honour, that the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was to be officially dismantled by the Washington agreement from April 1994, and in particular the Dayton peace agreement does not mention this entity at all, and provides for Bosnia-Herzegovina as being consisted only of two entities, namely Republika Srpska, the Serb Republic, on one hand, and the Federation of B & H on the other, with the clarification that constituent peoples in the federation are Bosniaks, i.e. Muslims, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I put it this way: until the coming into force of the Dayton agreement, would that provision have continued to be operated so far as the HZ H-B was concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor Pajic, time is growing short. I only have one question for you. What was the reaction at the time that all of these texts were proclaimed or drafted or came about, which were made official in the official journal, what was the reaction of Croatia? Were there any texts which allowed the different laws to be harmonised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Mr. President, from November 1991 until the summer of 1992 I did not travel to The Republic of Croatia, and so I can't be a good witness on the reactions to the establishment of HZ H-B as far as the public opinion, if you want, in the Republic of Croatia is concerned, but according to documents I analysed, there are a number of references where one could identify a certain degree of harmonisation of political interests and legal structures between The Republic of Croatia and HZ H-B entity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Professor Pajic, the Tribunal would like to thank you for remaining longer than you had planned in The Hague. The questions to be asked of Mr. Pajic have been asked. He can be ushered out of the courtroom. We again thank you and without any further ado we would like to say that we will continue in camera in order to move to this question which was raised after the pause by the Prosecutor. So the usher can take the witness out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you so very much. I have assumed my role in this Tribunal with great respect and as a great honour. Thank you very much. (Witness withdrew from court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Tribunal, that is the judges, will withdraw for several moments until the courtroom can be set up for the in camera hearing. (12.35 pm) (Short break) (In closed session)
